segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: As we saw in the last lecture, a major cause of climate change is the rapid rise in the level of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere over the last century.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: If we could reduce the amount of CO2, perhaps the rate of climate change could also be slowed down.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: One potential method involves enhancing the role of the soil that plants grow in, with regard to absorbing CO2.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Rattan Lal, a soil scientist from Ohio Stage University, in the USA, claims that the world’s agricultural soils could potentially absorb 13 per cent of the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere – the equivalent of the amount released in the last 3o years.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And research is going on into how this might be achieved.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Lal first came to the idea that soil might be valuable in this way not through an interest in climate change, but rather out of concern for the land itself and the people dependent on it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Carbon-rich soil is dark, crumbly and fertile, and retains some water.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But erosion can occur if soil is dry, which is a likely effect if it contains inadequate amounts of carbon.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Erosion is of course bad for people trying to grow crops or breed animals on that terrain.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: In the 1970s and ‘80s, Lal was studying soils in Africa so devoid of organic matter that the ground had become extremely hard, like cement.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: There he met a pioneer in the study of global warming, who suggested that carbon from the soil had moved into the atmosphere.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This is now looking increasingly likely.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Let me explain.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For millions of years, carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere have been regulated, in part, by a natural partnership between plants and microbes – tiny organisms in the soil.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Plants absorb CO2 from the air and transform it into sugars and other carbon-based substance.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: While a proportion of these carbon products remain in the plant, some transfer from the roots to fungi and soil microbes, which store the carbon in the soil.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The invention of agriculture some 10,000 years ago disrupted these ancient soil-building processes and led to the loss of carbon from the soil.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: When humans started draining the natural topsoil, and ploughing it up for planting, they exposed the buried carbon to oxygen.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This created carbon dioxide and released it into the air.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And in some places, grazing by domesticated animals has removed all vegetation, releasing carbon into the air.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Tons of carbon have been stripped from the world’s soils – where it’s needed – and pumped into the atmosphere.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So what can be done?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Researchers are now coming up with evidence that even modest changes to farming can significantly help to reduce the amount of carbon in the atmosphere.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Some growers have already started using an approach known as regenerative agriculture.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This aims to boost the fertility of soil and keep it moist through established practices.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: These include keeping fields planted all year round, and increasing the variety of plants being grown.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Strategies like these can significantly increase the amount of carbon stored in the soil, so agricultural researchers are now building a case for their use in combating climate change.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: One American investigation into the potential for storing CO2 on agricultural lands is taking place in California.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Soil scientist Whendee Silver of the University of California, Berkeley, is conducting a first-of-its-kind study on a large cattle farm in the state.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: She and her students are testing the effects on carbon storage of the compost that is created from waste – both agricultural, including manure and cornstalks, and waste produced in gardens, such as leaves, branches, and lawn trimmings.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: In Australia, soil ecologist Christine Jones is testing another promising soil-enrichment strategy.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Jones and 12 farmers are working to build up soil carbon by cultivating grasses that stay green all year round.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Like composting, the approach has already been proved experimentally; Jones now hopes to show that it can be applied on working farms and that the resulting carbon capture can be accurately measured.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It’s hoped in the future that projects such as these will demonstrate the role that farmers and other land managers can play in reducing the harmful effects of greenhouse gases.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For example, in countries like the United States, where most farming operations use large applications of fertiliser, changing such long-standing habits will require a change of system.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Rattan Lal argues that farmers should receive payment not just for the corn or beef they produce but also for the carbon they can store in their soil. Another study being carried out...
